summary:
SAR Change Watch is an interactive web map that turns NISAR radar images into stories anyone can read. For each (a wildfire, a monsoon flood, a glacier collapse, a river flood) it compares two NISAR L-brand images taken before and after, measures what changed on the ground, and shows it on a map with a before/after swipe.

It answers the challenge by tracking and visualizing several types of surface change (burn scars, flooding, ice and rock collapse) at locations on three continents. It then goes one step further: it explains the change. a guided story walks the viewer through each event step by step, with real photos, plain-language explanations and the measured numbers.

It matters because radar sees through cloud, smoke and darkness, which is exactly when disasters happens and cameras fail. But radar images are hard to read. We built this so that a student, a journalist or a local official can understand what NISAR saw without knowing anything about radar.
details:
What it does

- Before/after map. Shows two NISAR radar dates side by side with a draggable divider.

- Two views. "Only changes" colours the spots that changed: darker (water, mud, smoothed ground), double bounce (trunks, walls, blocks), rougher or greener ground, and wind on water. "Before & after" colours both dates by what the land was: water, bare ground, fields, bright surfaces.

- Landscape 500 m layer. Reveals change too subtle for single pixels but consistent over hundreds of meters. A boreal burn is the clearest example.

- Numbered areas. Finds and outlines the places where change is concentrated, largest first.

- Guided stories. A card over the map tells each event in 5–7 steps. The map flies to each place, switches layers by itself and outlines the area. Each step has a headline, real photos, the radar's own before/after pictures and source links. Every story includes a "why radar and not satellite photos" step and ends with how the event changed the Earth.

- Plain language everywhere. Resting the mouse on any spot explains it in everyday words. Clicking a colour explains what it means and what usually causes it. The technical details are available but folded away.

Events included

- Thunder Bay 36 wildfire, Ontario, Canada (July–August 2026)

- Monsoon flooding at the Meghna–Padma confluence, Bangladesh (July–August 2026)

- The Langtang Lirung ice and rock collapse behind Nepal's August 2026 flood

- Limpopo River flooding at Chókwè, Mozambique (January 2026)

How it works

1. A Python pipeline reads NISAR L2 GCOV products directly from NASA's cloud archive, fetching only the part of each file that covers the study area.

2. It smooths radar speckle and computes the change between the two dates in decibels.

3. It flags change above a noise-based threshold.

4. It uses the two polarizations (HH and HV) to tell kinds of change apart. A rise mostly in HH means double bounce. A rise in both means a rougher or leafier surface.

5. An API serves the results, and a React web map displays them.

6. The pipeline adapts to the computer's memory, so it runs on a small laptop and uses full resolution on a larger machine.

Why we built it this way

- Stories, because a change map alone did not communicate. Our own first version showed coloured pixels, and people could not tell where the disaster was or what the colours had to do with it.

- Honesty about limits, because radar cannot see everything. We tested events that this method does not show well: a debris flow in a narrow gorge, deep earthquakes, low crops. The app says so plainly. The Thunder Bay story also shows a false alarm (wind on lakes) that the map detects and leaves out of its numbers.

- Plain language, because the challenge asks for a broad audience. Areas are also given as football pitches, and every colour and spot can explain itself.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

- Make NISAR data understandable to people outside remote sensing.

- Give educators and communicators a ready way to show what radar adds when cloud or smoke hides the ground.

- Provide an open-source base that others can extend with new events. Adding one takes two commands.

Tools and languages

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-imarthaccess; pytest for the 55 automated tests.

- Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet (react-leaflet).

- Tooling: uv, Bun, Git/GitHub.

Links

- Frontend: https://github.com/yusof-shkn/sars-frontend

- Backend: https://github.com/yusof-shkn/sars-backend
